slides.0.title: 🌋 Campania
slides.0.subtitle: A Symphony of Ancient Grapes and Volcanic Soils
slides.1.title: 🏛️ A Cradle of Ancient Wine Culture
slides.1.content:
Campania lies in southern Italy, facing the Tyrrhenian Sea, with Napoli (Naples) as its capital. It has deep links with Greek, Etruscan and Roman wine, and Roman Falernum was one of the greatest wines of antiquity — a “first growth” of its time.

🌋 Campania is known for its volcanic soils and around 100 native grape varieties, many found nowhere else; 3 of its 4 DOCGs are in Irpinia.

slides.2.title: 🗺️ Campania Key DOCG & DOC Interactive Map
slides.3.title: 🍷 Aglianico — King of the South
slides.3.content:
👑 “The Barolo of the South”

Aglianico is one of Italy’s “noble” red grapes, Campania’s signature variety and its most widely planted grape. Its name is often said to come from “Ellenico” (Hellenic). Its principal appellations are Taurasi and Aglianico del Taburno.

⚫ High tannin, deep colour

Thick skins with high tannin and anthocyanins; tight and powerful in youth, it needs time to soften.

Extremely age-worthy
🍋 High acidity

Naturally high acidity which, with the tannins, forms the backbone for long life. Taburno’s Aglianico Amaro is named for its pronounced acidity.

Acidity + tannin = ageing potential
🌋 Late-ripening, loves volcanic soil

A late-ripening grape that prefers volcanic soils. Main biotypes: Aglianico di Taurasi, Aglianico Amaro (Taburno), Aglianico del Vulture (Basilicata).

Aglianicone is not a biotype of Aglianico
slides.4.title: 🏆 Taurasi DOCG — Crown of the South
slides.4.content:
Taurasi DOCG (promoted in 1993, southern Italy’s first DOCG) lies in the inland hills of Irpinia in Avellino province and is one of southern Italy’s most prestigious appellations, often mentioned alongside Barolo and Brunello.

📋 DOCG rules

  • Aglianico 85% minimum
  • Min. 3 years ageing (including 1 year in oak)
  • Riserva: 4 years (including 18 months in oak)
  • Piedirosso is the traditional blending partner; both small barriques and large casks (botti) are used

📍 Location

  • 17 communes in Avellino province
  • Hills at 300-700 m
  • Moderated by the Calore river, wide diurnal range
  • Calcareous clays and marine limestone mixed with volcanic material

🍷 How the flavours evolve

  • Young, 1-5 years: black cherry, plum, powerful tannins
  • Mature, 6-15 years: leather, tobacco, garnet colour
  • Aged, 15+ years: black truffle, tar, dried roses
slides.5.title: 🍾 The Three White Musketeers
slides.5.content:
🥇 Fiano di Avellino DOCG

The most prestigious appellation for Fiano, Campania’s most noble white grape and among Italy’s finest.

  • Flavours: hazelnut, honey, pear, white peach, minerality
  • Character: complex and long-lived; needs bottle age to show its full potential
  • Winemaking: typically made in stainless steel

🥈 Greco di Tufo DOCG

Named after the village of Tufo; the most prestigious appellation for Greco. The soils are high in sulphur, and the wines are high in acidity and very mineral.

  • Flavours: lemon, orange peel, peach, minerality, almond
  • Character: stainless steel, no oak; flinty, smoky (sulfurei), textured
  • Best pairing: oysters, fried seafood

🥉 Falanghina del Sannio

Fresh, lively, easy-drinking whites from Campania’s most widely planted white grape.

  • Flavours: green apple, apricot, white flowers, light minerality
  • Character: stainless-steel fermentation keeps the fruit pure; a versatile food wine
  • Best pairing: pizza, mozzarella, fried seafood
slides.6.title: 🌋 Volcanic Wine Areas
slides.6.content:
Campania’s volcanic soils vary greatly with the age and state of the volcano (active, dormant, extinct), and include lava, lapilli, ash, tuff and pumice; loose volcanic sands where phylloxera cannot survive have preserved many old and ungrafted vines.

🌋 Vesuvio DOC — Mount Vesuvius

Vesuvius is still an active volcano; vineyards are on the lower and middle slopes, at 50-400 m
Lacryma Christi del Vesuvio is the historic name, now a sub-category of Vesuvio DOC with stricter rules
Dark, loose, sandy volcanic soils keep phylloxera out; the Bianco is based on Coda di Volpe and the Rosso on Piedirosso

🔥 Campi Flegrei DOC — the burning fields

West of Napoli, a large volcanic depression created by numerous successive eruptions
Deep, loose, sandy volcanic soils with no phylloxera and many old ungrafted vines
Two principal wines: Campi Flegrei Piedirosso (Per' e' Palummo) and Campi Flegrei Falanghina
slides.7.title: 🍷 Other Important Campania Wines
slides.7.content:
🌋 Lacryma Christi del Vesuvio

“Tears of Christ”, a sub-category of Vesuvio DOC with stricter rules; the name supposedly comes from a drip-filtration system used by 17th-century monks.

  • Area: the lower and middle slopes of Vesuvius (50-400 m)
  • Grapes: Coda di Volpe Bianca (white), Piedirosso (red)
  • Character: smoky minerality from the volcanic soils

🏔️ Aglianico del Taburno DOCG

Formerly a sub-zone of Sannio DOC, a separate DOCG since 2011 and one of Italy’s three most important Aglianico appellations.

  • Area: Monte Taburno, Benevento province
  • Character: the local biotype Aglianico Amaro, with pronounced acidity; calcareous clay and sandstone topped with volcanic material
  • Ageing: min. 2 years; Riserva 3 years (1 year in wood)

🔥 Campi Flegrei DOC

A volcanic depression west of Napoli, with many ungrafted old vines.

  • Character: loose, sandy volcanic soils where phylloxera cannot survive
  • Grapes: Falanghina Flegrea, Piedirosso
  • Best pairing: seafood, shellfish, oysters

🌿 Sannio DOC

Historic Sannio corresponds to Benevento province, Campania’s largest wine-producing district.

  • Grapes: Fiano, Greco, Coda di Volpe Bianca, Aglianico and more
  • Character: varied soils and mesoclimates and many styles; like Falanghina del Sannio DOC, it has 5 sub-zones
  • Producer: Cantina del Taburno (a good-value cooperative)
slides.8.title: 🏛️ Coastal and Northern Appellations (IWS Course Material)
slides.8.content:
🏛️ Falerno del Massico DOC

Created to revive the legacy of Roman Falernum, it covers roughly the same area as ancient Falernum: around Monte Massico and the foothills of Roccamonfina, with volcanic soil over limestone.

  • Bianco: Falanghina (Flegrea)-based
  • Rosso: Aglianico-based (with Piedirosso)
  • Primitivo: varietal Primitivo
  • Riserva: both reds, min. 2 years (1 year in wood)

🌳 Asprinio di Aversa DOC

Around Aversa in Caserta province, based on the local Asprinio grape; flat, fertile land with a tuff subsoil covered by volcanic material.

  • Training: the Etruscan Alberata Aversana, with vines trained up poplar trees
  • Rules: min. 85% Asprinio; 100% for spumante
  • Styles: still, frizzante, spumante

🏝️ Ischia DOC

“L'isola Verde” (the green island), with over 2,000 years of winemaking; Campania’s first DOC (1966) and among Italy’s earliest.

  • Vineyards: steep, narrow terraces supported by dry-stone walls
  • Whites: varietal Biancolella and Forastera
  • Red: Piedirosso (Per' e' Palummo)

🌊 Costa d'Amalfi DOC

Steep, rocky terraces held up by dry-stone walls; loose volcanic soil over dolomite bedrock, many ungrafted centenarian vines, and pergola as the typical training system.

  • White: Biancolella, Falanghina
  • Red: Piedirosso, Aglianico, Sciascinoso
  • Sub-zones: Furore, Ravello, Tramonti
slides.9.title: 🍽️ Napoli Food Pairing Guide
slides.9.content:
Campania is a birthplace of Italian cuisine: Pizza Margherita and Mozzarella di Bufala both come from here, and local wine and food pairings follow their own logic.

🍖 Taurasi DOCG × wild-boar ragù

High tannins cut through the fat and dark fruit echoes the sweet-sour tomato sauce — Campania’s classic pairing. Also good with roast leg of lamb or aged Pecorino.

🦞 Fiano di Avellino × lobster

The rich body matches the sweet lobster meat, and the hazelnut notes echo a butter sauce. Also good with grilled fish in lemon butter or white-truffle pasta.

🦪 Greco di Tufo × oysters and seafood

High acidity and minerality refresh the palate, and the sea-salt character echoes the oysters’ brininess. Also good with sushi, poached prawns and fried seafood.

🍕 Falanghina × Pizza Margherita

The tomato’s acidity resonates with Falanghina’s fresh acidity — a quintessential Italian match. Also good with Mozzarella di Bufala and fried seafood.
slides.10.title: 📜 Campania Wine History in Depth
slides.10.content:
Campania’s wine history runs from Greek colonisation to the modern revival.

“Falernum was one of the greatest wines of antiquity — a ‘first growth’ of its time”

8th c. BC

The Greeks found colonies

The Greeks established important settlements in Campania and introduced low bush-trained vines; in the 7th century BC the Etruscans expanded south, bringing vines trained in trees (alberata).

3rd c. BC

The age of Falernum

Falernum was produced on the slopes of Monte Massico from the 3rd century BC, in three tiers by vineyard site: Faustianum (mid-slope, the finest), Caucinum (the highest vineyards) and Falernum (low-lying). Amphorae were marked with origin, vintage and producer — one of the first appellations in history.

476–1861

From turmoil to unification

After the fall of the Roman Empire Falernum sank into obscurity and Campania saw continuous regime changes; the Spanish Bourbons brought stability in the 18th century (the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies), and in 1861 Campania became part of the Kingdom of Italy.

1950s–1968

Mastroberardino and Taurasi

In the early 20th century Taurasi wines were shipped in bulk to northern Italy and France; two world wars and phylloxera devastated the industry. In the 1950s Antonio Mastroberardino focused on Aglianico, Greco and Fiano, having saved Fiano from extinction in the late 1940s; in 1968 he released a Taurasi Riserva.

1966–2011

DOC and DOCG

In 1966 Ischia became Campania’s first DOC; Taurasi became a DOC in 1970 and in 1993 southern Italy’s first DOCG; Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo (2003) and Aglianico del Taburno (2011) followed as DOCGs.

slides.11.title: 🍇 Campania’s Native Grapes in Full (IWS Course Material)
slides.11.content:
🍇 Around 100 native varieties, many found nowhere else

Campania kept its rich varietal diversity mainly because volcanic soils stopped phylloxera from spreading. In recent years outsiders such as Barbera, Sangiovese and Malvasia Bianca di Candia have been falling out of favour.

🔴 Red grapes

Aglianico: the most planted red grape — see the earlier slide. Piedirosso (Per' e' Palummo): an ancient grape historically grown around Napoli (Campi Flegrei, Vesuvio, Ischia, the Sorrento Peninsula); traditionally used to soften Aglianico and often grown on its own roots in volcanic soils. Others include Casavecchia, Pallagrello Nero, Sciascinoso and Tintore.

🥇 Fiano

Campania’s most noble white grape; first mentioned in the 13th century on a wine list for Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II; its ancient Latin name is Apianum. On the verge of extinction in the late 1940s, it was saved by Mastroberardino. Complex and long-lived, it needs bottle age.

The most noble white
🥈 Greco

An ancient white grape historically grown around Tufo; its name probably refers to an ancient Greek style of wine (with residual sugar) rather than a Greek origin. Late-ripening, difficult to grow, high in phenolics and acidity, age-worthy; it grows a double bunch and is prone to oxidation.

High acidity, prone to oxidation
🥉 Falanghina

An ancient native and Campania’s most widely planted white grape; revived in the 1970s by Villa Matilde, Mustilli and Grotta del Sole. It is in fact two genetically distinct varieties: Falanghina Flegrea (Napoli, Caserta) and Falanghina Beneventana (Benevento, the most widely planted).

One name, two varieties

Other white grapes: Biancolella (native to Ischia, moderate alcohol and acidity), Coda di Volpe Bianca (blended with Greco, Fiano or Falanghina, also varietal in Sannio and Irpinia), Asprinio, Forastera, Pallagrello Bianco. Note: Casavecchia is a red grape.
slides.12.title: 🌋 Topography, Climate, Soils and Training (IWS Course Material)
slides.12.content:
Campania’s topography is irregular, largely hilly and mountainous, facing the Tyrrhenian Sea. The coast is Mediterranean, becoming more continental inland; the Southern Apennines offset the southern latitude, and the hills have a big diurnal range.

🪨 Soils: diverse and complex

Mostly volcanic: they differ greatly with the age and state of the volcano (active, dormant, extinct)
Materials: lava, lapilli, ash, tuff, pumice; airborne material can travel far and mix with limestone, clay and sand
Phylloxera: loose, gravelly volcanic soils where phylloxera cannot survive, often with very old and/or ungrafted vines

🌿 Traditional training systems

Alberata: vines trained on or between trees, from the Etruscans; Alberata Aversana is the traditional training of Asprinio di Aversa (up poplar trees)
Raggiera: radial training, called starza in Taurasi; Guyot and cordone speronato are now more common
Pergola: overhead trellis, typical of Costa d'Amalfi; northern Ischia also uses pergola and alberata, while the south uses alberello, cordone speronato and Guyot
slides.13.title: 🔄 Taurasi: Traditional and Modern Winemaking
slides.13.content:
Taurasi winemaking balances traditional large casks and modern French barriques; each philosophy has its champions and great wines.

🏛️ Traditional

  • Ageing in large casks (botti)
  • Long maceration (20-30 days) for deep colour
  • Spontaneous fermentation with native yeasts
  • Minimal intervention
  • Traditional training: raggiera (locally called starza)

Examples: Mastroberardino, Antonio Caggiano

🔬 Modern

  • French barriques (225 L)
  • Precise temperature control (26-28°C)
  • Guyot and cordone speronato training
  • Shorter maceration (12-18 days) to keep the fruit
  • Rules: min. 3 years’ ageing (1 year in wood)

Examples: Feudi di San Gregorio, Terredora

⏳ How Taurasi ages

3 yrs
🍒
Dark fruit opens up, tannins begin to soften

20+ yrs

Leather and cigar, amber hues — legendary
slides.14.title: 🍾 The Three Great White Appellations (IWS Course Material)
slides.14.content:
🍇 The whites of Irpinia and Sannio

3 of Campania’s 4 DOCGs are in Irpinia (Avellino province); Sannio (Benevento province) is Campania’s largest wine-producing district.

🥇 Fiano di Avellino DOCG

Min. 85% Fiano (most are 100%), with Greco, Coda di Volpe Bianca and Trebbiano Toscano allowed; soils rich in clay and volcanic material; typically made in stainless steel. Four renowned villages: Summonte (concentration and power), Montefredane (mineral and long-lived), Lapio (pronounced aromatics), Cesinali (delicate and approachable).

Needs bottle age
🥈 Greco di Tufo DOCG

Min. 85% Greco with max. 15% Coda di Volpe Bianca (most are 100% Greco). Main villages Tufo, Santa Paolina and Montefusco, at 300-650+ m; clay mixed with limestone, sand and volcanic material, high in sulphur. Stainless steel, no wood: high acidity, mineral, flinty, smoky.

Sulphur-rich soils = smoky minerality
🥉 Falanghina del Sannio DOC

Min. 85% Falanghina, mainly the most widely planted Falanghina Beneventana. Like Sannio DOC it has 5 sub-zones: Guardiolo, Sant'Agata dei Goti, Solopaca, Solopaca Classico and Taburno. Mostly still wines, but also spumante and passito.

Falanghina Beneventana
slides.15.title: 🏰 Leading Campania Producers
slides.15.content:
Campania’s top estates follow different philosophies — from the legendary pioneer of 1878 to the academic estate of 2001 — and together shape southern Italy’s international image.

🥇 Mastroberardino (1878)

  • Antonio Mastroberardino is considered the father of modern Campanian wine
  • Saved Fiano from extinction in the late 1940s and also championed Aglianico and Greco
  • Released a Taurasi Riserva in 1968
  • Flagship: Radici Taurasi

🥈 Feudi di San Gregorio (1986)

  • A modernist benchmark estate in Irpinia
  • Focused on Fiano, Greco and Aglianico
  • Flagship: Serpico Irpinia Aglianico

🎓 Quintodecimo (2001)

  • Founder Luigi Moio: professor of oenology at the University of Naples
  • In Mirabella Eclano, focused on Irpinia’s Aglianico, Fiano and Greco
  • Flagship: Terra d'Eclano Taurasi

🏺 Antonio Caggiano (1990)

  • A family estate in the town of Taurasi
  • Known for single-vineyard Taurasi
  • Flagship: Vigna Macchia dei Goti Taurasi

🌱 Terredora di Paolo (1978)

  • The other branch of the Mastroberardino family (Walter Mastroberardino)
  • Focused on Irpinia’s three DOCGs
  • Flagships: CampoRe Taurasi, Pago dei Fusi Taurasi

🏛️ Villa Matilde (1960)

  • A pioneer of Falerno del Massico, the DOC created to revive the legacy of Roman Falernum
  • Led the Falanghina revival in the 1970s with Mustilli and Grotta del Sole
  • Flagship: Falerno del Massico Rosso

slides.17.title: 🎓 Key Takeaways
slides.17.points.0: ✓ Campania faces the Tyrrhenian Sea and is mostly hilly and mountainous; Mediterranean on the coast, continental inland, with a big diurnal range in the hills
slides.17.points.1: ✓ The Greeks brought low bush training and the Etruscans alberata; Roman Falernum (Monte Massico) was one of the greatest wines of antiquity
slides.17.points.2: ✓ Volcanic soils are varied; loose volcanic soils keep phylloxera out, preserving around 100 native grapes and many ungrafted old vines
slides.17.points.3: ✓ Aglianico (the Barolo of the South) is the most planted grape: thick-skinned, late-ripening, high in tannin and acidity, extremely age-worthy; Falanghina is the most planted white
slides.17.points.4: ✓ Taurasi DOCG (1993, southern Italy’s first DOCG): min. 85% Aglianico, min. 3 years (1 in wood), Riserva 4 years (18 months in wood)
slides.17.points.5: ✓ Aglianico del Taburno DOCG (2011): Aglianico Amaro, min. 2 years, Riserva 3 years (1 in wood)
slides.17.points.6: ✓ Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo both require min. 85% and are made in stainless steel; Fiano is the most noble white, and Greco di Tufo is known for flinty, smoky notes from sulphur-rich soils
slides.17.points.7: ✓ Ischia was Campania’s first DOC (1966); Lacryma Christi is a sub-category of Vesuvio DOC; Antonio Mastroberardino is considered the father of modern Campanian wine

slides.18.questions.4.options.0: Light and easy, with no ageing potential

slides.18.questions.6.question: Which of the following is NOT a biotype of Aglianico?
slides.18.questions.6.explanation: The three main biotypes of Aglianico are Aglianico di Taurasi, Aglianico Amaro (Taburno) and Aglianico del Vulture (Basilicata); Aglianicone is a separate red grape.
slides.18.questions.7.question: “Per’ e’ Palummo” is another name for which grape?
slides.18.questions.7.explanation: Piedirosso, also called Per’ e’ Palummo, is an ancient red grape from around Napoli, traditionally used to soften Aglianico and often grown on its own roots in volcanic soils.
slides.18.questions.8.question: Which auxiliary grape may make up to 15% of Greco di Tufo DOCG?
slides.18.questions.8.explanation: Greco di Tufo DOCG requires min. 85% Greco with max. 15% Coda di Volpe Bianca (most wines are 100% Greco); it is typically made in stainless steel with no wood.
slides.18.questions.9.question: What is alberata?
slides.18.questions.9.explanation: Alberata means training vines on or between trees, a method introduced by the Etruscans; Asprinio di Aversa’s Alberata Aversana trains vines up poplar trees. Low bush training came with the Greeks.
